title: Minimum Loss
directAnswer: Lauren buys a house in one year and must sell it in a *later* year at a *loss* (sell price < buy price); minimize that loss. Pair each price with its year, sort by price, and look only at consecutive prices in sorted order: for a sorted pair (lower, higher), it's a legal trade exactly when the higher price's year comes *before* the lower price's year — then the candidate loss is higher − lower. The minimum such difference is the answer. O(n log n) from the sort; prices reach 10¹⁶ so use long.

remember.pattern: Sort by price; minimal loss lives between consecutive prices
remember.formula:
pair (price, year); sort by price asc
best = +inf
for k in 1..n-1:
    hi = sorted[k], lo = sorted[k-1]
    if year(hi) < year(lo):   # bought higher earlier, sold lower later
        best = min(best, price(hi) - price(lo))
return best
rules: You **buy first, sell later** — the higher (buy) price must have the **earlier** year; the lower (sell) price the later year.
The minimum loss always occurs between **two consecutive prices** in sorted order — no need to check non-adjacent pairs.
All prices are **distinct**, so 'consecutive in sorted order' is well-defined and the difference is strictly positive.
Keep the original **year/index** alongside the price when you sort — that's how you check the buy-before-sell ordering.
Prices reach 10¹⁶ — use **long** (64-bit) for prices and the loss, an int overflows.
whenToUse: Minimize a positive difference between two elements subject to an ordering (time) constraint
'Closest pair' style questions where adjacency in sorted order limits candidates
Buy-low/sell-high or buy-high/sell-low with a temporal direction
antiSignals: No ordering constraint between the two elements → it's just min adjacent difference after sorting
Many queries / streaming inserts where you need the best so far each step → an ordered set (TreeSet) is cleaner than a one-shot sort
You may sell at a profit too → this is the classic max-profit stock problem, a different DP/greedy
remember.takeaway: Sort by value and only adjacent pairs can give the minimum difference. Carry the original index so you can enforce the time ordering, and the loss-minimization collapses from O(n²) pair-checking to a single O(n) scan after the sort.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realize that after sorting by price, the minimum loss must be between two consecutive prices — and that you still need the original years attached to enforce 'buy earlier, sell later'.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing all O(n²) pairs, forgetting the temporal direction (buy must precede sell), or using a 32-bit int when prices reach 10¹⁶.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Argue why only adjacent sorted prices matter: any non-adjacent valid pair has a price between them that forms a smaller valid difference. Mention the TreeSet streaming variant and call out the overflow before coding.

problemStatement:
Lauren has a chart of the price of a particular house over the years. Each year she could buy the house and, in some **later** year, sell it. She is only interested in transactions that result in a **loss** — selling for strictly less than she paid.

Given the prices indexed by year, find the **minimum loss** Lauren can incur. It is guaranteed that at least one losing transaction is possible, and all prices are distinct.
constraints: At least one valid (buy earlier, sell later at a loss) transaction exists
understanding: We need two years i < j (i earlier) with price[i] > price[j], minimizing price[i] − price[j]. Brute force checks every ordered pair. The key observation: if we sort the prices, the smallest positive gap between a buy and a sell can only come from prices that are adjacent in sorted order — but we must keep each price's original year to verify the buy happened before the sell.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must the sale happen in a later year than the purchase?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Buy at an earlier index, sell at a later index. The higher (buy) price must therefore have the smaller original index.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is selling at a profit allowed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — only losing transactions count. We minimize a strictly positive loss, never a gain.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are prices guaranteed distinct?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That makes sorting unambiguous and every adjacent difference strictly positive.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can prices get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 10¹⁶, which exceeds the 32-bit range. Use 64-bit integers for prices and the computed loss.

approaches.complexityReasoning: Two nested loops over all i < j → n(n−1)/2 ≈ n²/2 pairs, O(n²).
approaches.explanation:
The literal reading of the problem: a valid trade is a pair of years i < j where price[i] > price[j], and the loss is price[i] − price[j]. Enumerate every such pair and keep the smallest loss.

**Why both conditions matter.** `i < j` enforces buy-then-sell in time; `price[i] > price[j]` enforces that it's a loss, not a gain. Drop either and you count illegal trades.

**Use long throughout.** Prices reach 10¹⁶, so both the values and the differences must be 64-bit. A 32-bit int silently wraps.

**Why we don't ship it.** With n up to 2×10⁵, n²/2 ≈ 2×10¹⁰ comparisons — far too slow. Sorting reveals that only a handful of candidate pairs ever matter.
approaches.insight: Most of the O(n²) pairs are wasteful: a buy price that's far above the sell price can never be the *minimum* loss. Only prices close in value can produce a small loss — which is precisely what sorting surfaces.

approaches.name: Sort by Price + Adjacent Scan (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want: sort prices, keep years, and only consecutive sorted prices can be the minimum loss.
hints: If two valid prices are far apart in value, can their gap be the minimum loss? What if some other price sits between them?
Sort the (price, year) pairs by price. For a consecutive pair, the smaller difference is between adjacent prices.
A consecutive pair (lower, higher) is a legal trade only when the higher price's year is earlier than the lower price's year. Take the min of those differences.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting dominates at O(n log n). The adjacent scan is one O(n) pass. Storing (price, year) pairs is O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Sort the prices ascending, carrying each price's original year. Now walk consecutive pairs. For a sorted pair `(lower, higher)`, the only way it's a valid trade is to **buy the higher price and sell the lower** — and that requires the higher price's year to be *earlier* than the lower price's year. If so, the candidate loss is `higher − lower`.

**Why only adjacent pairs matter.** Suppose the optimal trade buys at price H and sells at price L with H > L. Take any other price X with L < X < H. If X's year is before L's year, then buying X and selling L is also valid and gives a *smaller* loss (X − L < H − L) — contradicting optimality. Otherwise X's year is after L's year; but X < H, and if X's year is after the buy year of H then selling X (instead of L) against H... the careful version of this argument shows the minimum loss is always realized by two prices with **no other price strictly between them** — i.e. consecutive in sorted order. So we never need non-adjacent pairs.

**Why we keep the year.** Sorting by price throws away the time order, but the trade legality depends entirely on it. Storing `(price, year)` lets us check `year(higher) < year(lower)` in O(1) per pair.

**Why long.** Prices reach 10¹⁶; the differences do too. Use 64-bit for the stored prices and the running best.

**Streaming variant (TreeSet).** Equivalently, process prices in year order while maintaining an ordered set of prices seen in earlier years. For each new (sell) price, query the smallest stored price strictly greater than it (a higher, earlier buy) and take that difference. Same O(n log n), handy when prices arrive one at a time.
approaches.insight: Sorting converts a global 'compare every pair' into a local 'compare neighbors' problem — the minimum gap between any two values is always between adjacent values once sorted. The only twist here is the temporal constraint, which we preserve by carrying the original index. This 'sort then look at neighbors' move is the backbone of closest-pair and minimum-difference problems.

code.python:
def minimum_loss(price: list[int]) -> int:
    # original index = year; sort indices by their price
    order = sorted(range(len(price)), key=lambda i: price[i])
    best = float('inf')
    for k in range(1, len(order)):
        hi = order[k]       # index of the higher price
        lo = order[k - 1]   # index of the lower price
        if hi < lo:         # higher price bought in an earlier year
            best = min(best, price[hi] - price[lo])
    return best

Legal trade: the higher (buy) price must occur in an earlier year than the lower (sell) price.
Adjacent sorted prices give the smallest possible positive gap.

pitfalls: Sorting only the prices and losing the original years — you can't check buy-before-sell.
Checking the wrong direction: it must be year(higher) < year(lower), not the reverse.
Using int for prices/loss — 10¹⁶ overflows; use long.

commonMistakes: Comparing all O(n²) pairs instead of adjacent sorted prices.
Dropping the original year, so the buy-before-sell constraint can't be enforced.
Using a 32-bit int when prices reach 10¹⁶.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Losing the year when sorting
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Sorting only the price values discards the time order, so you can no longer tell whether the higher price was bought earlier than the lower price was sold.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: order = sorted(range(len(price)), key=lambda i: price[i])  # keeps years

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong temporal direction
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A valid loss buys the HIGHER price first and sells the LOWER price later. Checking year(lower) < year(higher) flips the trade and counts impossible transactions.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: 32-bit overflow on prices
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Prices go up to 10¹⁶, far beyond Integer.MAX_VALUE (~2.1×10⁹). Storing or subtracting them as int corrupts the result.

patternNote: Sort-then-neighbors for minimum difference, plus an index carried through the sort to honor an ordering constraint. The minimum positive gap between values is always between adjacent sorted values; a TreeSet gives the streaming version. Same backbone as Minimum Absolute Difference and closest-pair problems.
